questions.question: Why use a requests.Session and explicit timeouts, and how do you configure them?
questions.title: Requests Sessions and Timeouts
questions.direct_answer: A requests.Session keeps cookies and default settings across calls and can reuse pooled connections to the same host. A timeout prevents a slow connection or stalled response from waiting indefinitely. Set timeout on each call, using either one value or a (connect, read) tuple; Session does not add a default timeout by itself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Session state and pooling, plus connect/read timeout semantics.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a Session creates a default timeout or that read timeout is a total download deadline.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name both the connection-reuse benefit and the mutable-state ownership boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Session can reuse connections and persist cookies across requests.
Session headers and auth provide shared defaults that per-call values can override.
Requests has no default timeout; pass one on every network call.
timeout=(connect_seconds, read_seconds) separates connection and socket-read waits.
A Requests timeout is not a guaranteed wall-clock deadline for the whole download.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A `requests.Session` groups related HTTP calls. It can persist cookies and shared settings such as headers or authentication, and it owns a connection pool that may reuse a connection to the same host. A timeout solves a different problem: it limits how long a network stage may wait.

The first request may need DNS lookup, a TCP connection, and TLS setup. After the response body releases that connection, a later call to the same host can reuse it. Session defaults are merged with each call, so a request can add or override a header without changing every future request.

Requests does not set a timeout automatically, and Session has no general default-timeout property. Pass one on every network call. `timeout=(3.05, 10)` gives separate connect and read values; a single number applies to both. The read value measures socket inactivity, not the total download time.

The example owns one Session with a context manager, sets headers once, and makes two page requests with the same explicit timeout. The function still checks every response before using its JSON. In tests, a stub Session can verify the URLs, parameters, and timeout without opening a socket.

support.title: Fetch two pages through one bounded Session
support.code:
import requests

def fetch_two_pages(base_url: str, token: str) -> list[dict]:
    with requests.Session() as session:
        session.headers.update({
            "Accept": "application/json",
            "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}",
        })
        orders = []
        for page in (1, 2):
            response = session.get(
                f"{base_url}/orders",
                params={"page": page},
                timeout=(3.05, 10),
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            orders.extend(response.json())
        return orders
support.caption: The Session owns reusable state; each individual call still owns an explicit waiting limit.

beats.recallRule: Use Session for related state and connection reuse, and set a timeout on every actual request.

sections.title: Connection reuse, shared request state, and time limits
sections.content:
Opening a connection can involve DNS resolution, TCP establishment, and TLS negotiation. Reusing a live connection avoids some of that work on later requests. Session manages this pooling and also provides a home for defaults, but it should have a clear ownership and lifecycle.

The timeout tuple names two different waits. Connect covers establishing a connection to a remote address. Read measures waiting for response data after the request has been sent; it is effectively an inactivity timeout between received bytes, not a stopwatch for the entire response.

Session state is mutable. Shared cookies, headers, and authentication are convenient within one client boundary but can leak context if an unrelated tenant or user reuses the same Session incorrectly. Close the Session, preferably with a context manager, when its owner is done.

sections.title: Connection reuse and timeout stages
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Python client
  participant S as Session pool
  participant A as API
  C->>S: first GET (connect timeout)
  S->>A: open connection and send
  A-->>S: response bytes (read timeout)
  S-->>C: Response
  C->>S: second GET
  S->>A: reuse pooled connection
  A-->>C: Response
```

questions.question: When should a Python API client use a requests.Session instead of one-off requests?
questions.title: Session vs One-Off Requests
questions.direct_answer: Use a Session for multiple related calls that benefit from connection reuse, shared cookies, authentication, or headers. A one-off requests.get() is fine for an isolated call with no shared state. Keep a Session inside a clear client lifecycle and do not accidentally share user-specific state across unrelated callers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Choosing a client lifetime that matches one isolated call or several related calls.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating one Session per call or sharing user-specific cookies across unrelated callers.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Sessions centralize policy but do not automatically add retries or response validation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: One isolated call does not require a Session.
Repeated calls to the same service can benefit from pooled connection reuse.
Session is the right place for service-wide headers, auth, and cookies.
Per-request arguments can override Session defaults.
Close Sessions and keep tenant- or user-specific state from leaking across callers.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Use `requests.Session()` when several calls belong to one API client or workflow and benefit from shared headers, authentication, cookies, or connection reuse. For one isolated public request, `requests.get(...)` is often simpler. The remote HTTP behavior is the same; the difference is client state and lifetime.

A one-off call creates little visible state but repeats configuration when calls multiply. A Session keeps that policy together and can reuse pooled connections, but it becomes a mutable object that needs an owner. Creating a new Session for every call loses most of the reuse benefit.

Keep the Session inside a clear service-client, job, or user boundary. A global Session that is mutated for different users can leak cookies or authorization headers. Per-request values may override defaults, but distant code should not casually change shared state. A `with requests.Session()` block closes it when that owner finishes.

The example accepts an owned Session, uses it for two related pages, and keeps timeout, status checking, and JSON decoding visible on each call. A Session does not automatically add retries, a timeout, or response validation. Those rules remain explicit even when connection and header setup are shared.

support.title: Use one owned Session for a paged API operation
support.code:
import requests

def fetch_item_pages(client: requests.Session, base_url: str) -> list[dict]:
    items = []
    for page in (1, 2):
        response = client.get(
            f"{base_url}/items",
            params={"page": page},
            timeout=5,
        )
        response.raise_for_status()
        items.extend(response.json())
    return items

with requests.Session() as client:
    client.headers["Accept"] = "application/json"
    items = fetch_item_pages(client, "https://api.example.com")
support.caption: The context manager gives the shared connection and header state a visible end to its lifetime.

beats.recallRule: Use a Session when related calls need reusable state; keep its ownership as narrow as that state.

sections.title: The lifetime and boundary of a Requests session
sections.content:
Module-level requests.get() uses a short-lived convenience path. Session makes the transport adapter and state visible as an object whose lifetime can match an API client. This is valuable when policy and reuse matter across calls.

Defaults are merged rather than frozen. A Session header can be supplemented or overridden for one request. That flexibility is useful, but it makes ownership important: a shared mutable client should not be casually changed in distant code.

Connection reuse is scoped by the underlying pool and destination. Creating a fresh Session for every call defeats that benefit. Keeping one global Session for unrelated authentication contexts creates a different problem. A service client or unit-of-work boundary is usually a clearer middle ground.

sections.title: Match client lifetime to call pattern
sections.content:
| Call pattern | One-off function | Session |
|---|---|---|
| Single independent request | Simple fit | Usually unnecessary |
| Several calls to one API | Repeats setup | Reuses pool and defaults |
| Cookies/login flow | Manual continuity | Persists cookies |
| Multiple user identities | Separate calls can isolate state | Use separate owned Sessions |
| Timeout policy | Explicit per call | Still explicit per call |

sections.title: Worked Python example
sections.content:
```python
import requests

def health_status(url: str) -> int:
    # One independent request can use the convenience function.
    return requests.get(url, timeout=3).status_code

def fetch_two_pages(base_url: str) -> tuple[dict, dict]:
    # Related requests share one owned Session.
    with requests.Session() as client:
        client.headers["Accept"] = "application/json"
        first = client.get(f"{base_url}/items", params={"page": 1}, timeout=5)
        second = client.get(f"{base_url}/items", params={"page": 2}, timeout=5)
        first.raise_for_status()
        second.raise_for_status()
        return first.json(), second.json()
```

questions.question: What is the difference between connect and read timeouts in Requests?
questions.title: Connect Timeout vs Read Timeout
questions.direct_answer: The connect timeout limits waiting to establish a connection to a remote address. The read timeout limits how long Requests waits for response data after connection, more precisely the inactivity between bytes. Neither is a strict deadline for the complete request, and multiple address attempts can extend elapsed time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Where connect and read timeouts apply and why elapsed wall time can be longer.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing timeout=(3.05, 10) as a strict thirteen-second total deadline.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect a timed-out write to its potentially ambiguous server-side outcome.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Connect timeout covers establishing the network connection.
Read timeout covers waiting between bytes from the server.
timeout=(3.05, 10) sets connect and read values separately.
A single timeout value is applied to both stages.
These values are not a total wall-clock deadline for the operation.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The connect timeout limits waiting to establish a connection to a remote address. After the connection is ready and the request is sent, the read timeout limits how long Requests waits without receiving response bytes. They protect different stages, so their values often need to differ.

With `timeout=(3.05, 10)`, the first value is the connect timeout and the second is the read timeout. An unreachable destination can raise `ConnectTimeout`; a connected server that stops delivering bytes can raise `ReadTimeout`. Both belong to the broader `Timeout` exception family.

A read timeout is an inactivity limit, not a maximum duration for the complete response. A long stream can continue while bytes keep arriving inside each interval. Connect time is also applied per address attempt, so a hostname with multiple addresses can take longer overall than one connect value suggests.

The function translates connect and read failures into different messages and leaves the original exception as the cause. Tests can inject a client that raises each exception without waiting on a network. A timed-out write is still ambiguous: the server may have completed it, so timeout handling alone does not make a retry safe.

sections.title: Connect and read timeouts protect different waits
sections.content:
A single phrase such as 'the request timed out' can hide where progress stopped. Separating connect and read stages produces more useful diagnostics and lets a client tolerate an intentionally slow response without waiting too long for an unreachable host.

DNS, address selection, proxies, TCP, and TLS can affect observed connection time. Requests documents connect timeout per connection attempt, so wall-clock behavior can be longer than the tuple suggests. Read timeout is also socket-oriented: it observes gaps in received bytes rather than total processing duration.

An application with a strict end-to-end deadline may need a higher-level cancellation or task deadline in addition to Requests timeouts. It must also close or abandon downstream work safely when that deadline expires.

sections.title: Where each timeout applies

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant A as API
  Note over C,A: connect timeout
  C->>A: establish connection
  C->>A: send HTTP request
  Note over C,A: read timeout measures gaps between response bytes
  A-->>C: response chunk
  A-->>C: next response chunk
```
